The Truth Behind Playoff Hockey

Do goalies decide who makes the playoffs?

Author

Ben Buchler

Published

June 4, 2026

Introduction

What makes NHL teams playoff worthy? While watching this year’s NHL playoffs, I couldn’t help but wonder what sets these teams apart. Two teams with virtually the same players on paper can have incredibly different outcomes over the course of an 82 game season. The difference I realized can come down to one position, the goaltender. An exceptional performance in this years NCAA frozen face off triggered this idea for me.

University of Denver goaltender Johnny Hicks. With 49 saves against Michigan and 29 against Wisconsin Johnny Hicks played a big role in the pioneers victory. Johnny had a save percentage of 0.967 playing every minute of the game and since stepping in at the end of January. Ever since Hicks took the net the pioneers haven’t lost a game. If a goaltender change can lead a team on a 17 game winning streak what effect can goalies have on the NHL level.

The blog investigates the statistical effect a goaltender can have on making the NHL playoffs, and compares the effect to the impact of raw goal scoring. To do so, I compiled three seasons of NHL play-by-play data from the hockeyR package alongside three seasons of individual goalie statistics from MoneyPuck.com. Using all these data sets I was able to examine my question from both the team and the individual perspective.

I address these two more specific sub-questions in my analysis:

  1. How correlated is team goalie save percentage with making the playoffs?
  2. How correlated is team goal-scoring with making the playoffs?

This type of data analysis gets me excited because it has real value. Front offices look at data like this when building rosters, forecasting playoff chances. Analytics like this could even be used for fans sports betting.

Data

Sources

This analysis calls on two data sets spanning the 2021–22, 2022–23, and 2023–24 NHL seasons:

  • hockeyR play-by-play data (pbp_combined): This has Event-level data for every regular season and playoff game, including event type, team, expected goals (xg), and game identifiers.
  • MoneyPuck.com goalie data (goalies): Season-level statistics for goaltenders, shots on goal, goals allowed, ice time, and high-danger shots. Each goalie-season contains rows for several game situations.
Show code 
library(hockeyR)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(broom)
library(knitr)
library(scales)
Show code 
pbp_combined <- bind_rows(
  mutate(hockeyR::load_pbp(2022), across(everything(), as.character)),
  mutate(hockeyR::load_pbp(2023), across(everything(), as.character)),
  mutate(hockeyR::load_pbp(2024), across(everything(), as.character))
) |>
  type.convert(as.is = TRUE)

goalies24 <- read.csv("~/Sports Analytics/Sports Analytics/goalies.csv")
goalies23 <- read.csv("~/Sports Analytics/Sports Analytics/goalies (1).csv")
goalies22 <- read.csv("~/Sports Analytics/Sports Analytics/goalies (2).csv")

goalies <- bind_rows(goalies22, goalies23, goalies24)
Show code 
clean_df <- function(df) {
  df |>
    remove_empty("cols") |>
    remove_empty("rows")
}

pbp_combined <- clean_df(pbp_combined)
goalies      <- clean_df(goalies)

goalies_all <- goalies |>
  filter(situation == "all")

Dataset Overview

Key variables used in this analysis:

Dataset Variable Description
pbp event_type Type of play (GOAL, SHOT, etc.)
pbp season_type R = regular season, P = playoffs
pbp home_abbreviation Home team abbreviation
pbp xg Expected goals value per event
goalies goals Goals allowed by the goalie
goalies ongoal Shots on goal faced
goalies icetime Total ice time in seconds
goalies games_played Games played
goalies highDangerShots High-danger shots faced

Exploratory Data Analysis

Before addressing my main hypothesis I wanted to see the distribution of goalie performance across my data collected sample. The chart below shows save percentage for goalies that played over 1,000 minutes across the three seasons.

Show code 
goalies_all |>
  filter(icetime > 1000, ongoal > 0) |>
  mutate(save_percent = 1 - (goals / ongoal)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = save_percent)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(save_percent, na.rm = TRUE)),
             color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(
    title    = "NHL Goalie Save Percentage Distribution",
    subtitle = "Red dashed line = median | Seasons 2022–2024",
    x        = "Save Percentage",
    y        = "Number of Goalie-Seasons"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

The distribution is roughly bell shaped and centers around 90%. There is a spread however, some goalies lie above 93% will other preform worse below 88%. This means there is potential for save percentage to be a predictive value.

The chart below shows the average expected goals per game for the top 20 organizations in the regular season.

Show code 
pbp_combined |>
  filter(season_type == "R", !is.na(xg), event_team != "") |>
  group_by(event_team) |>
  summarise(avg_xg = mean(xg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(avg_xg > 0) |>
  slice_max(avg_xg, n = 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(event_team, avg_xg), y = avg_xg)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title    = "Top 20 Teams by Average Expected Goals per Event",
    subtitle = "Regular season | 2022–2024",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Average xG per Event"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

The margin of expected goals between teams is noticeably small. This could suggest that expected goals and the quality of a teams offense does not weigh heavily in a teams playoff chances. This gives me more confidence that goalies can be a deciding factor.

Analysis 1 — Save Percentage and Playoff Probability

Building the Data

Show code 
goalie_team <- goalies_all |>
  filter(ongoal > 0, icetime > 0, season %in% c(2022, 2023)) |>
  mutate(
    save_pct = 1 - (goals / ongoal),
    gaa      = (goals / icetime) * 3600
  ) |>
  group_by(team, season) |>
  summarise(
    avg_sv_pct  = mean(save_pct,    na.rm = TRUE),
    average_goals_per60     = mean(gaa,         na.rm = TRUE),
    total_games = sum(games_played, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups     = "drop"
  )

# Source: hockey-reference.com/playoffs/2022 and /2023
playoff_teams <- tibble(
  team = c(
    # 2021-22 Eastern Conference
    "BOS", "CAR", "FLA", "NYR", "PIT", "TBL", "TOR", "WSH",
    # 2021-22 Western Conference
    "CGY", "COL", "DAL", "EDM", "LAK", "MIN", "NSH", "STL",
    # 2022-23 Eastern Conference
    "BOS", "CAR", "FLA", "NJD", "NYI", "NYR", "TBL", "TOR",
    # 2022-23 Western Conference
    "VGK", "EDM", "LAK", "SEA", "DAL", "MIN", "WPG", "COL"
  ),
  season        = c(rep(2022L, 16), rep(2023L, 16)),
  made_playoffs = 1L
)

goalie_playoff <- goalie_team |>
  left_join(playoff_teams, by = c("team", "season")) |>
  mutate(made_playoffs = replace_na(made_playoffs, 0))


goalie_playoff |>
  count(made_playoffs) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Made Playoffs", "Team-Seasons"),
    caption   = "Playoff vs. non-playoff team-seasons in the sample."
  )
Playoff vs. non-playoff team-seasons in the sample.
Made Playoffs Team-Seasons
0 32
1 32

The output from the data above may be a little confusing. The data is showing that over the course of 2 seasons 32 teams made the playoffs and 32 team didn’t between 2021 and 2023.

Correlation Test

Show code 
cor_sv <- cor.test(goalie_playoff$avg_sv_pct, goalie_playoff$made_playoffs)

tibble(
  Statistic = c("Correlation (r)", "p-value"),
  Value = c(round(cor_sv$estimate, 4), formatC(cor_sv$p.value, format = "e", digits = 3))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Correlation between total goals and playoff appearance.")
Correlation between total goals and playoff appearance.
Statistic Value
Correlation (r) 0.3639
p-value 3.113e-03

The correlation coefficient is 0.364 with a p-value of 0.00311, indicating a statistically significant positive relationship between team save percentage and playoff appearance.

Logistic Regression

Because made playoffs is binary, logistic regression estimates the probability of making the playoffs as a function of team save percentage.

Show code 
model_sv <- glm(made_playoffs ~ avg_sv_pct,
                data   = goalie_playoff,
                family = binomial)

tidy(model_sv) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Logistic regression: playoff appearance ~ average team save percentage.")
Logistic regression: playoff appearance ~ average team save percentage.
term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) -55.2153 20.6594 -2.6727 0.0075
avg_sv_pct 61.1653 22.8808 2.6732 0.0075

Visualization

Show code 
ggplot(goalie_playoff, aes(x = avg_sv_pct, y = made_playoffs)) +
  geom_smooth(
    method      = "glm",
    method.args = list(family = binomial),
    color       = "red",
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("Did not make playoffs", "Made playoffs")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Does Save Percentage Predict Playoff Appearance?",
    subtitle = "Each point = one team-season | Seasons 2022–2024",
    x        = "Team Average Save Percentage",
    y        = NULL,
    caption  = "Sources: hockeyR, MoneyPuck.com"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

The logistic regression shows a positive relationship between save percentage and making the playoffs. Teams with higher save percentages are more likely to reach the postseason. This supports the idea that goal tending can mask poor offensive and defensive performances throughout the year.

Analysis 2 — Goal Scoring and Playoff Probability

The second question asks whether raw goal-scoring power is similarly predictive. If offensive players drive playoff odds as much as goal tending, teams would prioritize acquiring powerhouse goalscorers.

Building the Data

Show code 
team_lookup <- c(
  "Anaheim Ducks" = "ANA", "Arizona Coyotes" = "ARI", "Boston Bruins" = "BOS",
  "Buffalo Sabres" = "BUF", "Calgary Flames" = "CGY", "Carolina Hurricanes" = "CAR",
  "Chicago Blackhawks" = "CHI", "Colorado Avalanche" = "COL", "Columbus Blue Jackets" = "CBJ",
  "Dallas Stars" = "DAL", "Detroit Red Wings" = "DET", "Edmonton Oilers" = "EDM",
  "Florida Panthers" = "FLA", "Los Angeles Kings" = "LAK", "Minnesota Wild" = "MIN",
  "Montreal Canadiens" = "MTL", "Nashville Predators" = "NSH", "New Jersey Devils" = "NJD",
  "New York Islanders" = "NYI", "New York Rangers" = "NYR", "Ottawa Senators" = "OTT",
  "Philadelphia Flyers" = "PHI", "Pittsburgh Penguins" = "PIT", "San Jose Sharks" = "SJS",
  "Seattle Kraken" = "SEA", "St. Louis Blues" = "STL", "Tampa Bay Lightning" = "TBL",
  "Toronto Maple Leafs" = "TOR", "Vancouver Canucks" = "VAN", "Vegas Golden Knights" = "VGK",
  "Washington Capitals" = "WSH", "Winnipeg Jets" = "WPG"
)

goals_team <- pbp_combined |>
  filter(event_type == "GOAL",
         season_type %in% c("R", "REG", "2"),
         season %in% c(20212022L, 20222023L),
         !is.na(event_team), event_team != "") |>
  mutate(
    season = as.integer(season) %% 10000L,
    team = team_lookup[event_team]
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(team)) |>
  group_by(team, season) |>
  summarise(total_goals = n(), .groups = "drop")

goals_playoff <- goals_team |>
  left_join(
    playoff_teams |> mutate(season = as.integer(season) %% 10000L),
    by = c("team", "season")
  ) |>
  mutate(made_playoffs = replace_na(made_playoffs, 0))

Correlation Test

Show code 
cor_goals <- cor.test(goals_playoff$total_goals, goals_playoff$made_playoffs)

tibble(
  Statistic = c("Correlation (r)", "p-value"),
  Value = c(round(cor_goals$estimate, 4), formatC(cor_goals$p.value, format = "e", digits = 3))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Correlation between total goals and playoff appearance.")
Correlation between total goals and playoff appearance.
Statistic Value
Correlation (r) 0.6692
p-value 2.745e-09
Show code 
model_goals <- glm(made_playoffs ~ total_goals,
                   data   = goals_playoff,
                   family = binomial)

tidy(model_goals) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Logistic regression: playoff appearance ~ total regular season goals.")
Logistic regression: playoff appearance ~ total regular season goals.
term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) -19.1399 4.7008 -4.0716 0
total_goals 0.0734 0.0179 4.0991 0

When looking at the correlation and regression the correlation is 0.669 much higher than the correlation on the goalies analysis. Additionally, the P value is exponentially below the threshold deeming it significant.

Visualization

Show code 
ggplot(goals_playoff, aes(x = total_goals, y = made_playoffs)) +
  geom_smooth(
    method      = "glm",
    method.args = list(family = binomial),
    color       = "violet",
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("Did not make playoffs", "Made playoffs")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Does Goal Scoring Predict Playoff Appearance?",
    subtitle = "Each point = one team-season | Seasons 2022–2023",
    x        = "Total Goals Scored (Regular Season)",
    y        = NULL,
    caption  = "Source: hockeyR"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

This logistic regression also shows a positive correlation between goals scored and making the playoffs. The curve is steeper in this model suggesting a stronger relationship between goals and getting to the playoffs.

Comparing Both Models

To determine what is a better predictor I decided to use AIC of both logistic regression models. A lower AIC indicates a better-fitting model relative to the number of parameters used.

Show code 
tibble(
  Model = c("Save Percentage", "Goals Scored"),
  AIC   = round(c(AIC(model_sv), AIC(model_goals)), 2)
) |>
  arrange(AIC) |>
  kable(caption = "Model comparison by AIC. Lower AIC = better fit.")
Model comparison by AIC. Lower AIC = better fit.
Model AIC
Goals Scored 54.31
Save Percentage 83.35

Goals scored has a lower AIC than save percentage suggesting that scoring is more important than saving when it comes to winning games. This aligns with the other comparisons above and points to a different conclusion from my original hypothesis.

Top Goalie Performers

Before going into discussion of my results I think it is important to note players that made an impact across these seasons and compare it to teams that made the playoffs.

Show code 
goalies_all |>
  filter(icetime > 12000, ongoal > 500, goals > 0) |>
  mutate(
    save_percentage = 1 - (goals / ongoal),
    season = as.integer(season)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(save_percentage)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  left_join(playoff_teams, by = c("team", "season")) |>
  mutate(
    made_playoffs = replace_na(made_playoffs, 0),
    made_playoffs = ifelse(made_playoffs == 1, "✅ Yes", "❌ No"),
    save_percentage = percent(save_percentage, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  select(name, team, season, save_percentage, goals, ongoal, made_playoffs) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Goalie", "Team", "Season", "Save %", 
                  "Goals Against", "Shots on Goal", "Made Playoffs?"),
    caption = "Top 10 NHL goalies by save percentage and shots on goal and whether their team made the playoffs."
  )

When you look at this data it still gives me confidence in my original hypothesis as the goalies that saw the most shots on goal and had the highest save percentage almost all went to the playoffs. The two most impressive goalies on this tibble are Linus Ullmark and Conner Hellebuyck in my opinion as they both saw over 1500 shots and maintained a save percentage in the 90s. Additionally, Conner Hellebuyck appears twice and in both scenarios saves over 90% of a substantial amount of shots.

Discussion

This analysis set out to answer two questions: does goalie save percentage predict playoff success, and/or does goal scoring? Both show positive relationships with making the playoffs, but the comparison reveals an interesting story about what matters most.

Team save percentage showed to have a positive correlation with the postseason. Teams with high performer goaltenders were more likely to make the playoffs. This shows in the top goalies performers above. The goalies with the highest save percentage that saw the most shots almost always made it to the playoffs. The logistic regression plot shows a steady upward curve that becomes more pronounced as goalie save percentage surpasses the average in the league. This supports my initial intuition that great goal tending can sustain a team through a challenging regular season even when lacking in the defense and offense departments.

Goal scoring also showed a significant correlation between goals and making the post season. In hockey teams that score more goals are generally better teams. The AIC model shows that goals are a better predictor of playoff hockey teams. Goals had and AIC of 54 and Save Percentage had and AIC of 83. Although both goals and saves are good predictors for being a good team it is clear goals are more important.

There are some limitations in this analysis to acknowledge. Only taking three seasons of data is a small sample size despite how much data is within each season. If I were to do this analysis again I would have selected at least 8 seasons of data to ensure sharper accuracy. The goalie data is aggregated at the team level, which can mask situations where one dominant starter carries a roster while a backup struggles. Additionally, constructing the playoff indicator from the home games column in the data could have introduced some biases as not all teams play the same amount of games at home. Finally, I ran into some issues joining my data for analysis two and ultimately had to hard code what teams made the playoffs based on a new data set from 2022 and 2023. If I were to do this project again I would change my methods to analyze individual goalies vs individual high scorers to attempt to further build a case for the importance of goalies in th NHL.

The bottom line is that goalies are important to winning games. The numbers support it and they are even meaningful statistical predictors for playoff success.
